hook.line: "You don't have to" and "you can't" are worlds apart, but both lean on the same frame in Spanish. Say the wrong one to a guest and you either lock the door or leave it wide open.
hook.en: You don't need to come. (to a friend)

examples.en: You don't need to come. (to a friend)
It is forbidden for you to go in. (to a friend)

examples.es: No hace falta que traigas nada.
examples.en: You don't need to bring anything. (to a friend)
It is forbidden for you to bring food. (to a friend)

examples.es: No hace falta que pague hoy.
examples.en: You don't need to pay today. (formal)

examples.es: Está prohibido que los niños pasen a la cocina.
examples.en: It is forbidden for children to go into the kitchen.

rule:
Both start with a short phrase, then *que*, then the changed verb ending: *vengas*, *entres*, *traigas*. Only the opening phrase decides the meaning.

*No hace falta que…* means it is not needed. The door is open: do it if you like.

*Está prohibido que…* means it is not allowed. The door is shut.

Watch the English trap. "You don't have to" is *no hace falta*. "You mustn't" is *está prohibido*. Quick test: if the person does it anyway, is that fine? Yes means *no hace falta*, no means *está prohibido*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the difference between absence of obligation and prohibition. Both take the present subjunctive after *que*.

options: You don't need to come.
You're not allowed to come.
You must come.
You don't need to go in.
You must go in.
You're not allowed to go in.

yourTurn.prompt: A friend is welcome but not obliged. Pick *No hace falta* or *Está prohibido*, then type the whole sentence: *___ que vengas.*
yourTurn.why: Nothing is banned, so the door is open: *no hace falta*.

yourTurn.prompt: A sign on the staff door. Pick *No hace falta* or *Está prohibido*, then type the whole sentence: *___ que entres.*
yourTurn.why: It is a ban, so the door is shut: *está prohibido*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: You don't need to bring anything.
yourTurn.answer: No hace falta que traigas nada.
yourTurn.why: A host being kind says *no hace falta que* plus the changed ending *traigas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: It is forbidden for you to bring food.
yourTurn.why: A ban on a person uses *está prohibido que* and the same changed ending.

yourTurn.prompt: Switch it to a ban. *No hace falta que pagues hoy.* Say, to a friend: It is forbidden for you to pay today.
yourTurn.why: Swap only the opening phrase; *que pagues* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Switch it to not needed. *Está prohibido que los niños pasen a la cocina.* Say: Children don't need to go into the kitchen.
yourTurn.answer: No hace falta que los niños pasen a la cocina.
yourTurn.why: Swap only the opening phrase; *que los niños pasen* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to someone you call *usted*: You don't need to pay today.
yourTurn.answer: No hace falta que pague hoy.
accept: No hace falta que usted pague hoy.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *que* the verb takes the changed ending: *vengas*, not *vienes*.

pitfalls.wrong: No hace falta que fumes aquí.
pitfalls.why: Almost. "You mustn't" is not "you needn't": for a ban, use *está prohibido*.

pitfalls.right: No hace falta que traigas nada.
pitfalls.why: Almost. A kind host is not banning anything, so "you don't need to" is *no hace falta*.

personal: Imagine a friend coming to your place this weekend. Tell them one thing they don't need to do (*No hace falta que…*) and one thing that is not allowed (*Está prohibido que…*).
